title: Identifying Reasons Behind a Speaker's Points
keyIdea: When someone speaks to persuade you, listen for three parts. The point (or claim) is what they want you to agree with. A reason says why. Evidence is a fact, number or example that backs up a reason. Then check: is each reason about the point, is the evidence enough, and does the point really follow?

kid: When people speak to persuade you, they make a point. A point is what they want you to think or do. "We should plant a school garden" is a point.

A good speaker gives reasons. A reason says why. "A garden would help us learn science outside" is a reason. Evidence backs up a reason with a fact, a number or a real example: "In Year 3 we grew beans and measured them every day."
Signal words help you spot each part. "Because" and "first" often bring a reason. "For example" and "according to" often bring evidence. "So" often comes just before the point.

Then judge it. A reason must be about the point, not just the same topic. One or two examples are not enough to say "everyone". An opinion is not evidence. If you are not sure, ask: "What evidence supports that?" or "Could there be another reason?"
adult: This is a Speaking and Listening standard for ages 9 to 10 (Common Core SL.4.3): identify the reasons and evidence a speaker gives to support particular points. In the English National Curriculum it sits in spoken language. Children listen and respond, ask relevant questions and give clear explanations. Useful terms are point or claim, reason, evidence, signal words, relevant and logical.

Children first need to hear the shape of an argument: one point, a few reasons, and evidence for each reason. Listening is harder than reading, because spoken words are gone at once. Short talks help. So do signal words and a simple map: the point at the top, reasons below, and evidence under each reason.

Watch for common mistakes. Children call an example a reason. They treat any sentence on the same topic as support, such as "I love lunch" for a longer lunch break. They accept an opinion as evidence, or jump from one or two cases to "everyone". They miss a link that does not follow. A quick check: put "because" between the reason and the point. Does it still make sense?

In the lab your child sorts a short council talk into point, reasons and evidence. Then they tap signal words, decide which claims support a point, name what is wrong with weak reasoning, and pick the follow-up question that tests a claim.

familyTip: Watch a short advert or listen to a news clip together. Ask: what do they want us to think? What reasons do they give? Is there any evidence, or just opinion? Take turns asking one good follow-up question.

visual.caption: Point: "Our school should have a longer lunch break." Is each line a reason or evidence? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: We need time to eat and still play
Playing outside helps us focus in the afternoon
The queue is so long we can't finish
Last Monday, 40 children were still eating at 12:55
In our survey, 9 out of 10 pupils said lunch is too short
According to the cook, the queue takes 15 minutes

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort a talk into point, reasons and evidence, tap signal words, test if claims support a point, judge reasoning and ask a probing question.

practice.prompt: "We should have a class pet because it would teach us to care for animals." What is the reason?
choices: It would teach us to care for animals
We should have a class pet
practice.hint: The reason answers "why?". Look after the word "because".
practice.explain: "It would teach us to care for animals" says why. "We should have a class pet" is the point. "Because" is the signal word.

practice.prompt: A speaker says: "For example, {n} children came to the book club last week." What is this?
practice.hint: Is it a fact or example, or what the speaker wants?
practice.explain: It is evidence: a real number ({n} children) that backs up a reason. "For example" signals it.

practice.prompt: Point: "Our playground has only {n} bins. We need more bins." Which claim supports it?
choices: Litter blows around because the bins are always full
practice.hint: The claim must help show we need more bins.
practice.explain: Full bins and blowing litter show there are not enough bins. Bin colour and a tidy bedroom are off the point.

practice.prompt: "My friend got sick after eating cheese, so cheese is bad for everyone." What is wrong with the reasoning?
practice.hint: How many people does the evidence come from?
practice.explain: One friend cannot show something is true for everyone. That is too few examples to support "everyone".

practice.prompt: Which signal word usually brings in evidence?
practice.hint: Which one leads to a real case or fact?
practice.explain: "For example" brings in a real case that backs up a reason. "Firstly" often starts a reason, and "however" brings in a contrast.

pool.prompt: In a talk, what is the point?
choices: What the speaker wants you to agree with
A fact with a number in it
pool.hint: Think of the big idea the whole talk is about.
pool.explain: The point (or claim) is what the speaker wants you to think or do. Reasons and evidence support it.

pool.prompt: "The library should open at lunch. According to Mrs Lee, {n} pupils asked to borrow books at lunch." Which part is evidence?
choices: {n} pupils asked to borrow books at lunch
The library should open at lunch
pool.hint: Evidence is a fact or example. "According to" only tells you where it comes from.
pool.explain: The fact about {n} pupils is the evidence, and Mrs Lee is the source. The first sentence is the point.

pool.prompt: Point: "Our town needs a new park." Which is off the point?
choices: Children have nowhere safe to play
The nearest park is 3 miles away
pool.hint: Which one does not help show the town needs a park?
pool.explain: "Parks can be very old" is about parks, but it does not show this town needs one. The other two are reasons and evidence.

pool.prompt: "Red is the nicest colour, so our team shirts should be red." What is wrong?
choices: The reason is just an opinion
pool.explain: "Nicest colour" is an opinion, not evidence. People can disagree, so it does not prove the point.

pool.prompt: "It rained on sports day, so we should stop doing PE." What is wrong?
choices: The point does not follow from the reason
It has evidence from a survey
pool.hint: Say "because" between them. Does it make sense?
pool.explain: One rainy sports day has nothing to do with stopping PE. The point does not follow.

pool.prompt: A speaker says: "Video games make children unkind." Which follow-up question tests the reasoning best?
pool.hint: A good question checks the reason or the evidence.
pool.explain: "What evidence supports that?" asks the speaker to back up the claim. The others do not test it.

pool.prompt: "In our survey, {n} out of 30 pupils walk to school, so we need a safer crossing." Is this strong?
choices: Yes: it has evidence that fits the point
No: it is just an opinion
pool.hint: Is there a fact? Is it about the point?
pool.explain: The survey gives a fact ({n} out of 30 walk), and many walkers is a fair reason for a safe crossing. That is strong.

pool.prompt: "Our team lost because the pitch was wet." Which question asks about other explanations?
choices: Could there be another reason you lost?
pool.hint: Look for a question that asks whether the reason is the only one.
pool.explain: Asking for another reason tests whether the wet pitch really caused the loss. Maybe the other team played better.
